<<European Skies and the Tower of Change>>

Section 1
EasyJet reported a record year for passenger numbers—80.2 million people flown on fuller planes—but profits before tax fell from £494m to £408m, a drop the airline blamed partly on more than £100m wiped out by the slump in sterling after the Brexit vote. Revenues topped £5bn even as fares dipped to fill seats in what CEO Carolyn McCall described as “a difficult year for the aviation industry.” She pointed to the carrier’s strategy of holding number one or two positions at Europe’s leading airports, friendly and efficient service, and tight cost control as reasons easyJet remained resilient while some rivals struggled. Forward bookings and stronger revenue for the new financial year lifted shares, and the board said some capacity leaving the market had helped performance so far.

Section 2
Brexit prompted a legal scramble: to ensure ongoing access to EU routes, easyJet will tighten its rules so it is majority owned and controlled by EU nationals after 2019. About a third of shares are held by founder Stelios Haji-Ioannou, who has UK-Cypriot nationality and will be classed as EU-owned. Nonetheless, the airline will seek new powers at its 2018 AGM to compel changes in share ownership if necessary, including forcing some UK shareholders to sell to secure its European licence. McCall called the measures “a technical, administrative thing” and said the company had no concerns about attracting sufficient EU ownership. Investors treated the update as reassuring, sending shares up by more than 5% in early trading.

Section 3
Beyond spreadsheets and briefings there is a human story: crew who dare to navigate tighter schedules, ground staff at a tower guiding denser traffic, and managers who must treat regulatory shifts as urgent practical challenges rather than abstract policy fights. For many passengers this was a year of expanded options—cheaper fares, more routes—but for industry society as a whole the upheaval was a test of adaptability. Executives spoke of trimming costs and pursuing strategic positions, while regulators and shareholders negotiated new rules. Like anglers adjusting their technique when the tide changes, airlines and airports have had to vary the old practice of simply expanding—sometimes the smartest move is to change how you fish, not only where.
